title: Mutex Lock
body:
A binary lock thats a pecial case of [[Semaphores]] (counter is either 0 or 1)

The name is short for **mut**ual **ex**clusion, which is precisely the one requirement it
enforces. 1 means the lock is free, 0 means somebody holds it. Acquire decrements, release
increments, and there is nowhere else the counter can go.

```C
acquire(&m);      // if 0, block into a Waiting state
// critical section
release(&m);      // set to 1 and wake a waiter
```

## Against a general semaphore

| | [[Mutex Lock]] | [[Semaphores]] |
|---|---|---|
| Counter range | 0 or 1 | 0 to *n* |
| Answers | "is anyone inside?" | "how many are left?" |
| Ownership | the thread that acquired it should release it | anyone can post it |
| Use | protect a [[Critical Section]] | count a resource: free slots, available items |

**A mutex cannot count, and that is the whole reason semaphores exist.** In
[[Producer Consumer]] the `mutex` semaphore keeps the two threads out of each other's way,
but it cannot tell the producer that the buffer is full; `slot_avail` counting down from *n*
does that. See [[Bounded Buffer Problem]].

The ownership row is the practical difference. A mutex is meant to be released by whoever
took it, which lets the kernel do things like priority inheritance. A semaphore is a signal
and posting one from a different thread is normal, which is exactly how the producer wakes
the consumer.

It still blocks rather than spins: a thread that cannot get the mutex goes into the
[[Waiting state]] on a [[Wait Queue]] instead of burning CPU. Compare [[Spin Lock]].

[[POSIX]] gives you `pthread_mutex_lock` and `pthread_mutex_unlock` for the real thing, and
`sem_init(&s, 0, 1)` builds the same behaviour out of a semaphore.
